Special Commission of Inquiry
into Healthcare Funding
Before: The Commissioner,
Mr Richard Beasley SC
At Level 2, 121 Macquarie Street,
Sydney, New South Wales
Thursday, 22 February 2024 at 10.00am
(Day 008)
Mr Ed Muston SC (Senior Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ross Glover (Counsel Assisting)
Mr Ian Fraser (Counsel Assisting_
Mr Dan Fuller (Counsel Assisting)
Dr Tamsin Waterhouse (Counsel Assisting)
Also present:
Mr Lachlan Gyles SC with Ms Joanna Davidson for NSW Health

THE COMMISSIONER: Good morning. Yes, Mr Fraser?
MR FRASER: Thank you, Commissioner. Commissioner, the
next witness to be called is Mitchell Clancy. I think,
unless anyone else has any other matters, we are ready to
proceed to Mr Clancy's evidence. We've taken the liberty
of putting him in the witness box.
<MITCHELL CLANCY, affirmed: [10.01am]
<EXAMINATION BY MR FRASER:
MR FRASER: Q. Mr Clancy, could you give your full name,
please?
A. Mitchell Clancy.
Q. And it is correct, isn't it, that you are the district
procurement manager for the South Western Sydney Local
Health District; is that right?
A. Correct.
Q. Mr Clancy, how long have you been in that role?
A. I'm now moving into my third year at South Western
Sydney.
Q. I didn't catch that. Was that third year or --
A. Third year, yes.
Q. Before you were in this role, what were you doing?
A. I was working at Western Sydney Local Health District
as an assets and compliance manager.
Q. So in the same field?
A. Yes.
Q. But effectively one rung down; is that correct?
A. Similar - well, same level, but different portfolio,
so mainly focusing on assets and engineering.
Q. As opposed to procurement?
A. Still procurement role but focused primarily on
engineering and similar type contracts.
Q. I believe you chair a number of committees; is that
right?
A. Correct.

Q. Within the district?
A. Yes.
Q. Are they the tender review committee?
A. Yes.
Q. And the strategic procurement advisory board?
A. Yes.
Q. And can you tell us what each of those do in general
terms?
A. Sure. Starting with the strategic procurement
advisory board, that's an executive level meeting whereby
we have local health district representatives, generally
executive, and we also have a Ministry of Health chief
procurement officer sitting on that committee and also
a HealthShare representative.
So basically it's a meeting where we discuss
procurement initiatives and once that has been discussed
and agreed upon, we then move into the formal procurement
process from there. And we also share data regarding
current procurement projects and brainstorm matters that
are new initiatives related to procurement in our district.
Q. Thank you. And the tender review committee obviously
has a role in relation to tenders?
A. Yes.
Q. But is that just district membership or --
A. It is district membership only, yes.
Q. And what does it actually do in relation to tenders?
A. So the role of the tender review committee is to
provide governance for all procurement activities completed
within South Western Sydney, and essentially, the role of
the TRC is to ensure value for money is achieved, probity
and procurement process has been adhered to, and just as an
external set of eyes to make sure we've got the best
outcome for the district.
Q. So is that a committee that is involved at the
beginning of the tender process, during - whilst a tender,
a request for tender, is being formulated, in the
evaluation, secondly, or the subsequent operation of the
following contract, or in all three or a combination?
A. It's generally at the very end of procurement

activities. So once the local procurement team have
conducted the tender, it then gets shared for the tender
review committee and they provide final endorsement that it
has achieved value for money, probity has been adhered to,
and it makes sense to have that contract in the district.
And from there, the tender review committee makes
a recommendation to the chief executive to allow the award
of the contract to that preferred vendor.
Q. And just in general terms, value for money, other than
what the dollar amount is, which is clearly a factor in
that --
A. Yes.
Q. -- what else is generally factored in to value for
money?
A. Look, predominantly it is just about money and
ensuring that there might be potential savings but also
reviewing any potential value-adds that might have been
tendered as part of that process, so it might be - as part
of procurement activity a tenderer might provide education
and training and extra potential support that might be
considered additional to what was normal practice.
Q. I will just ask you, are you familiar with the terms
"value based health care" and "value based procurement"?
A. Yes.
Q. And in looking at those - at value, do you look at
benefits that might not be directly financial?
A. Yes, we do look at things like work, workforce
efficiencies, which we do consider a saving or efficiency
for our district as part of that process.
Q. You manage a team; is that right?
A. Correct.
Q. I think they're termed - are they termed - your team
members, are they termed category managers?
A. Some are category managers and others are in different
roles to the category managers.
Q. How big is your team?
A. When it's at full capacity, 19FTE, within procurement
and I'm currently involved in fleet as well and
sustainability within our district.

Q. Fleet? Can you just keep your voice up a little,
maybe come a little bit closer to the microphone.
A. Sorry, sure.
Q. But that's a separate - fleet is a separate --
A. It's a separate function.
Q. -- function?
A. To procurement, yes.
Q. But 19 in procurement?
A. Yes.
Q. And between your team, you oversee all the procurement
within the district; is that right?
A. Correct, excluding some of the work that is done in
capital works and our redevelopment teams, but then I would
review that as part of our tender review committee process.
Q. I'll just leave capital works to one side. It's not
a - you have some oversight but not commissioning the
procurement itself - is that right - in shorthand?
A. Correct.
Q. In terms of your procurement, that includes
procurement done through both HealthShare and eHealth; is
that right?
A. Yes.
Q. Can we just focus on HealthShare first. If there's an
issue with a statewide contract, are you the point of
escalation?
A. From the local health district?
Q. From the local health district to HealthShare?
A. Yes, generally. But there are times when my category
managers will directly liaise with HealthShare as well.
Q. And what kinds of things get escalated to HealthShare,
either by you or a category manager.
A. There are several things, first one being vendor
performance. So if a vendor isn't performing to what we
consider to be satisfactory, and that can be in line with
some key performance indicators within our contracts, we'll
manage that locally, but when required we will escalate
that as that well to HealthShare for their assistance at
that state level.

Q. And are there other matters that tend to be the
subject of --
A. There is.
Q. -- escalation?
A. Assets, for example. So if some of our medical
imaging equipment goes down and there's an outage, we again
escalate that through to HealthShare because the vendors
are subject to key performance indicators on the state
contracts and when they don't meet those key performance
indicators we can receive abatements for that
non-performance.
Q. You mentioned medical imaging as an example there?
A. Yes.
Q. Whoever the contract for, say, ultrasound devices, is
with, if they break down more than a prescribed amount
within a certain period, then there's an abatement that is
due under the contract; is that right?
A. Yes. If they breach the KPI there is an abatement
payable to the districts.
Q. But that is raised with HealthShare, is it?
A. Yes.
Q. And no doubt is a matter that's relevant to whether
statewide contracts are awarded in the future?
A. Yes.
Q. You mentioned KPIs?
A. Mmm-hmm.
Q. All the statewide contracts have KPIs for suppliers;
is that right?
A. Correct.
Q. And they can cover a wide range of things presumably?
A. Yes.
Q. Such as timeliness in deliveries, breaking down of
equipment --
A. Yes.
Q. -- if it's equipment?
A. Yeah, complaints as well.

Q. Complaints as well?
A. Yes.
Q. And how are you aware of what the KPIs are for the
statewide contracts?
A. All the KPIs are listed in the state contracts which
are listed on Portt Discover, which is the state's contract
database.
Q. So that's the database for all the statewide health
contracts; is that right?
A. Correct.
Q. When you escalate concerns of one type or another to
HealthShare, how do you find the responsiveness from
HealthShare?
A. I would say good. They are very responsive to what we
do escalate and they are generally very willing to give us
a hand and work through negotiations or issue resolution as
required.
Q. Issue resolution?
A. If there's some sort of discrepancy or something we're
not happy with, they're a part of that process and they can
become a bit of a mediator as part of our process.
Q. Between --
A. Us.
Q. "Us" - you and the vendor?
A. Correct.
Q. Within your district, presumably there's sometimes
a product recall; is that right?
A. Correct.
Q. And if there's a product recall, perhaps the vendor
contacts, obviously, the district and says, "Look, this
batch of" - whatever it may be - "is subject to a recall".
Do you, within the district, have, at the moment, the
ability to trace items through to patients?
A. Yes, we can. So particularly for prosthetics, so we
use the h-trak program and that's our record of what
prostheses have been in which procedure, installed by the
clinician that did that work.

Q. So your district uses h-trak?
A. We do.
Q. We have heard some evidence already about h-trak,
thank you. What about DeliverEASE, has that been rolled
out in your district yet?
A. It has been partially rolled out. So we're fully
implemented at Liverpool Hospital.
Q. Fully rolled out at Liverpool?
A. Correct. And we're at 60 per cent for Bankstown
Hospital, no, sorry, disregard that. It was Fairfield
Hospital, and we're working through Bankstown and
Campbelltown Hospital in mid May.
Q. So it's in the process through Campbelltown - in the
other hospitals?
A. Correct.
THE COMMISSIONER: Q. Have you had any feedback about
DeliverEASE at Liverpool and whether it's improved things?
A. Yes, Commissioner. There's been positive feedback as
part of that installation or that implementation of
DeliverEASE. So we've got greater compliance with
infection control standards, which is good; we've got more
efficient ordering practices; and there's less
over-ordering. So we should have reduced our stock at
completion of that project as well.
Q. The staff that are using it feel as though it's an
improvement?
A. Yeah, that's the feedback that I've got. They're
happy with the program at the moment, yes.
MR FRASER: Q. So it's made differences, in your
opinion?
A. The feedback that I've received indicates that, yes,
it has, but we are in the process of doing a post-project
survey to get some data on that.
Q. So feedback has been informal but not formal yet; is
that right?
A. Yes.
Q. When do you expect it will be fully rolled out across
all the facilities in the district?
A. By the end of the financial year.

Q. I just want to ask you some questions in relation to
the tender process and the involvement of the district when
new statewide contracts are established or they're up for
review and renewal.
A. Mmm-hmm.
Q. Do you have a role in that, on behalf of the district?
A. I have a huge role in that, yes.
Q. Do you want to explain that, please?
A. So initially a business case will be developed of the
key stakeholders, to determine the business need for that
particular good or service. So that would generally be in
the form of a brief that is written to the chief executive
and that would detail what the business requirement is, the
current spend and details of procurement process that would
be undertaken.
Depending on the project, that will obviously be
discussed at the strategic procurement advisory board as
well and brainstormed, and then that will then get added to
the brief as well, that that's already been through that
process and has been endorsed by the SPAB.
From that process, we go into a very lengthy
procurement process but it's obviously dependent on the
level of spend required as part of the procurement process.
So when drafting that brief to the chief executive we do
what's called a "tender risk assessment" and that
determines the type of tender process we're to follow when
conducting that procurement activity. So if it's less than
$250,000 it's not as complex, but anything over $250,000 is
a more complex process where we're required to engage
HealthShare as part of that tender activity.
Q. Is it true that engagement - that sometimes a
procurement process might turn into a statewide contract?
A. Generally not - if it's being conducted by the
district it will not be a statewide contract, it will
purely just be a local procurement activity.
Q. At least from where you sit in the district, is it
clear to you how it's decided what things become the
subject of statewide contracts as opposed to district
procurements?
A. Yes.

Q. How does that occur?
A. When we complete a local procurement activity, that's
purely just for our district, but HealthShare manage all
the statewide contracts and the tendering process for that.
Q. Yes, but in terms of new statewide contracts, there's
a new technology?
A. Yes.
Q. Your clinicians have become aware of it and the
district wants it?
A. Yes.
Q. But it might be relevant to other districts across the
state. How does it come to the point where HealthShare
might say, "We're going to do this on a statewide level"?
Is that through your strategic procurement advisory board?
A. That would be probably the first point where that
would be discussed, because we've got ministry and
HealthShare as part of that board. So that will be shared,
"There's a business need here, there might be potential to
make that into a state contract." And then we'll open up
discussions with HealthShare and then we'll work through
the strategy. But after that point HealthShare takes over
that procurement activity and they come back to us for
advice on what they'd like to have involved or incorporated
into that procurement activity.
Q. Clearly, if it's going to be statewide they do the
process?
A. They do, yeah.
Q. If it's going to be a significant procurement but done
at a local level, it's - HealthShare have some oversight
but you're doing the process?
A. Correct.
Q. Where it's a statewide contract, and it has been
renewed or there's, for instance - or it's a new statewide
contract, what role do you have for the district?
A. So I would be part of the process in facilitating
either clinicians or other stakeholders that might be able
to participate in that statewide contract on behalf of
South Western Sydney Local Health District. And there may
be times when our own procurement staff will sit on those
statewide contracts to help ensure we get the best outcome

as part of that process.
Q. How do they do that?
A. Get the best outcome?
Q. Yes.
A. So you want to have subject matter experts involved in
all the decision-making when it comes to tendering. So if
it's - if you've got a piece of equipment that might be
biomedical equipment, you want to have a biomedical
engineer provide that advice on that statewide contract to
ensure we get the best outcome for health.
Q. So there's sometimes, effectively, experts from your
district that you, you know, link up the procurement
process with; is that right?
A. Correct.
Q. And they're involved in the evaluation process?
A. Yes.
Q. And sometimes that will be clinicians; is that right?
A. It will be clinicians, when it's a clinical type
product, for example, prostheses and other similar type
things, we will engage clinicians to ensure that they have
the opportunity to have input into the tender outcome.
Q. How do you identify them? Do you go to the relevant
department and --
A. We know who the subject matter experts are in our
organisation, but if we're not too sure, I'll send it out
to their stream manager or director and say, "I need
someone that can provide this input", and they'll know the
person that should be invited into that process.
Q. I would just like to ask you about statewide contracts
generally.
A. Sure.
Q. Once it's a statewide contract, effectively, you have
to use it; that's right, isn't it?
A. Yes, correct.
Q. Just in terms of your perspective, do you perceive
that your district, South Western Sydney, gets the best
value out of those contracts all the time?
A. I wouldn't say all the time. I think there is

definite opportunity to achieve further savings for metro
local health districts.
Q. Metropolitan districts?
A. Yes, because we are close to shipping and airports,
et cetera. So there is more efficiency for the vendors in
giving us better pricing rather than, say, for example,
shipping goods and services out west. So I think there are
definite opportunities to potentially do better in the
metro LHDs.
Q. Are there any particular areas that, you know, in your
mind, fall in that category?
A. Potentially medical imaging, where it's quite
expensive to put a large piece of medical imaging equipment
on a truck and transport it, whereas if it's coming off
a shipping container into a metro LHD, those costs would be
reduced.
Q. So it's really your perception of that saving is
particularly because of transport costs, shipping costs and
the like; is that right?
A. Correct.
Q. How would you see that working for metropolitan
districts? Would it be separate contracts or would it be
different provision and pricing structures within the
contracts?
A. I think having the ability to conduct local further
tender offers that are only applicable to the local health
district completing that activity is where you could get
greatest value for money. So at the moment, they've got
what's called "continuous best price", so if a vendor
offers a good price to our local health district, they may
be required to apply that across the whole entire state on
certain contracts.
Q. And you might not be able to answer this, but would
that potentially drive up the price for regional LHDs?
A. It could potentially. So the overall strategy is to
achieve best price across the district as a whole, and so
generally those far west local health districts, they
leverage off the back of the good pricing that is given to
metro LHDs.
Q. I would just like to ask you some questions now
generally about eHealth. Just one moment, if I may. So in

relation to, obviously, eHealth, they deal with information
technology equipment for the district?
A. Correct.
Q. And they don't just deal with procurement of
equipment, they also provide some services; is that right?
A. Yes.
Q. And are there services that you're required to comply
with or use?
A. I can't talk too much to eHealth and their services,
that's more the ICT. I can really talk more about the ICT
procurement and our relationship with eHealth, yeah.
Q. So in relation to that process, procurement, were
there any reflections you have on that process, of
procuring ICT things through eHealth? Does it cause any
difficulties for the district?
A. eHealth are quite rigid in their processes, and in
procurement there are more efficient ways to conduct
procurement that can honestly save money and time, and I'd
like to think that our team is quite mature in the way we
conduct our procurement activities and we know where we can
be more efficient. Where we do share those ideas, we don't
always necessarily get approval to do that work and that
might be because of their interpretation of what the policy
is, but we have a different interpretation on certain
aspects of what that policy actually states.
Q. Can you give us an example?
A. I might talk about direct negotiations. So under the
procurement policy there is ability to conduct direct
negotiations, if you've got a strong business case to do
so. For example, we're in the process of working through
a managed print service contract. And working through that
process with eHealth, we requested to do direct
negotiations with a vendor off the back that another LHD
recently conducted procurement activity. So rather than go
through that whole entire process and come to the same
outcome, we requested to do direct negotiations.
So once that was escalated to the senior exec within
eHealth that was approved but at that lower level it took
a fair bit of time and conversation to get to that point,
because they couldn't understand our strategy and what the
benefits actually were if we were to go through that
process.

Q. So you got there but it took quite a bit of time; is
that what --
A. It did, yes.
Q. Just in terms of the process of ICT procurement, it
differs a little to procurement through HealthShare; is
that right?
A. It does but it is very similar.
Q. Just as a general process, how does it operate?
A. I would say it is not as efficient as the HealthShare
process, so there's a lot more detail and information
required to get to market, compared to HealthShare, which
takes time.
Q. Which takes time?
A. Yes.
Q. And what is it that causes the need for more detail
and information than sort of a comparable procurement
through HealthShare?
A. I'm guessing - I speculate, potentially just because
the ICT procurement processes that they've got might be
different to the HealthShare ones but I'm not entirely
sure.
Q. Do all procurements of ICT equipment - at what level
does it require e health to be involved?
A. It does depend on the dollar value.
Q. In the same way as it does for HealthShare?
A. It does, yes. But I have an ICT category manager that
liaises very closely with eHealth on all matters ICT
procurement related.
Q. So are there any procurements you're able to just not
go to eHealth at all?
A. Sorry?
Q. Is there a low-value ICT procurement that you don't
need to engage with eHealth at all?
A. Yeah. For example, IT software below a certain
threshold, we're not required to engage the ICT - sorry,
the eHealth procurement team, but we still need to liaise
with eHealth on the cybersecurity aspect of that project.

Q. We'll come back to cybersecurity in a moment. Is
there then a level that you have to get approval from
eHealth and, as you have said, you are then able to do it
yourself, like the direct negotiation that you have just
mentioned?
A. This is a challenging part of our relationship at the
moment. So we do request to have the same approach as what
we do with HealthShare. So HealthShare have what's called
a level 1 or a tender light engagement whereby they purely
just manage the tender box and we run the full procurement
activity and everything goes in that tender box and we
liaise with HealthShare to provide them documentation and
everything else that's required as part of that procurement
activity, but we essentially run that activity.
Q. So they, effectively, oversight it?
A. They check, making sure that we're --
Q. They make sure that you're following the right
processes?
A. Yes.
Q. And the documents are there for them to see, but
you're doing it all?
A. Yes.
Q. Is there not an equivalent with eHealth?
A. eHealth prefer to be more hands-on, is my experience.
And we're now working through what that sort of looks like
and what sort of freedom we can have to conduct our
procurement activities because we have the intimate
understanding of what the procurement activity is. We've
got a very mature team in the way we conduct our
procurement activities, and when you rely on another party
to conduct the procurement activity it's dependent on their
time and their schedule.
Q. Is it not clearly set out in a policy as to what -
when you can do it yourself and when you can't?
A. It depends on the engagement that's listed by eHealth
and HealthShare. So that's dependent on - there's
a procurement policy that says we must engage them, but
that interpretation of how you engage them is what can be
interpreted in different ways. So we meet that requirement
with HealthShare via our tender light submission, sorry,
engagement, whereby they manage that tender box, and that
provides compliance with the procurement policy.

So we see the same thing with our relationship with
eHealth, we're still engaging them but we still - we think
we can run it more efficiently than what they can.
Q. But they don't relax control as much as HealthShare;
is that one way of putting it?
A. It's more challenging to get that freedom to conduct
that procurement activity with that vendor.
Q. Presumably there is large-scale ICT procurement --
A. Yes.
Q. -- as there is with HealthShare that has to be done
through eHealth?
A. Yes.
Q. For instance, if you were replacing the entire IT
system within the whole district, for instance?
A. Yes.
Q. I'll just come back to cybersecurity. What is it that
you have to engage with eHealth about in relation to
cybersecurity?
A. So for all goods and services related to ICT, there
needs to be a cybersecurity assessment done, which is
called - under the privacy security assessment framework.
Q. I think, there are some documents we've seen, I think
it might be the privacy security assurance framework.
A. Yeah. Yes.
Q. Is that something relatively new or is that --
A. It was released last year.
Q. So 2023. And that's an eHealth policy, is it?
A. It is.
Q. No doubt we can get that if we need to from eHealth.
What does it require?
A. It requires a security - a cybersecurity assessment
done for all ICT goods and services that would have some
sort of connection to our cloud or servers, et cetera.
Q. I see. And that includes, I think you said earlier,
your small-scale software procurement, so you need two
licences for Adobe, for instance?

A. Yes.
Q. There has to be an assessment of that done?
A. That's my understanding, yes.
Q. Even though it might be software that is being used in
every single LHD?
A. Yes. So we've been advised that we need to do
retrospective assessments as well for things that we're
currently using where an assessment hasn't been done.
Q. If it was something that was procured through eHealth
originally, presumably in that process it would have been
done by them - is that right - already?
A. Not necessarily.
Q. Not necessarily. All right. How does that
cybersecurity assessment get done? Who does it?
A. eHealth.
Q. And is there a charge for it?
A. There is a charge, dependent on the complexity of that
good or service.
Q. Before this policy of last year, how would that - did
this occur?
A. I can't talk to that too much because that was more of
an ICT remit. It's only really come to my knowledge when
we were completing a new procurement activity, that is
certainly a requirement that we need to conduct. So we do
have an in-house cybersecurity manager that can work
through those projects locally as well.
Q. So the fee varies depending on the complexity --
A. Yeah.
Q. -- which makes sense. And would you say that --
THE COMMISSIONER: But does the fee vary? Is that an
assumption or --
MR FRASER: I think that's what the witness said.
Q. Does the fee vary?
A. It should, but depending on the complexity, yes, so --
Q. It should, but does it?

A. It will. So we're still working through that now and
going through that process of what that looks like. So our
ICT team could probably provide more information on that.
Q. What sort of range is the fee?
A. Ten to $30,000 is what I've understood.
Q. Sorry, 10 to $30,000?
A. Yes.
Q. Are you resourced for that? Is there a funding stream
for that?
A. Not to my knowledge, no.
THE COMMISSIONER: Q. Is it charged as a lump sum for
doing a particular service or is there an hourly rate or --
A. I'm not sure, to be honest. I just - when we get that
initial - when we engage with eHealth on what that project
is, they give us, like, an indicative figure of "This is
what it should cost to complete that PSAF".
MR FRASER: Q. So, effectively, it becomes an additional
cost of the procurement?
A. Yes.
Q. For the new procurement?
A. Yes.
Q. And in terms of having to do retrospective
assessments, firstly, how long have you been given to do
them?
A. It's something that --
Q. Or have them done, I should say?
A. The chief information officer from our district would
probably be best placed to comment on that. I'm not aware
of a timeline but -- -
Q. And the fact that they're retrospective tends to
suggest that they're assessments that weren't done
previously?
A. Correct. Under that particular framework.
Q. So it may have been different assessments were done
but not those that met the requirements in the framework?
A. Potentially, yes.

Q. And in relation to the retrospective assessments, is
there any additional funding that has come to the district
that you are aware of?
A. Not that I'm aware of.
Q. And you referred to having - you have some in-house
ICT capability; is that right?
A. We do. Within the ICT team there's a cybersecurity
manager employed full time to conduct local assessments.
Q. To conduct these type of assessments?
A. That's what they're employed to do, is my
understanding.
Q. Is he able to conduct the assessments to satisfy this
policy?
A. The initial conversations I have had with that person
are yes, they can, and the chief information officer,
I believe, is discussing that with eHealth on what local
arrangements might be able to facilitate compliance with
that policy.
Q. So at the moment, to your knowledge, that's a matter
under discussion but hasn't been resolved?
